claims.text: The unchanged (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy has a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field cycling.
The unchanged alloy has poor mechanical integrity and is prone to crack propagation.
Melt infiltration with 10–20 vol% copper can form a bicontinuous copper–caloric-matrix composite.
A continuous ductile copper network will provide crack bridging and load transfer.
The bicontinuous structure will maintain intimate connectivity of the active caloric phase.
Copper is ductile and has high thermal conductivity.
The copper scaffold will limit crack initiation and propagation.
The copper scaffold will improve the composite's compressive strength.
A limited copper fraction will minimally interfere with the intrinsic caloric phase transformation.
Copper infiltration will preserve the alloy's large caloric response.
The copper-infiltrated composite will reach a compressive strength above approximately 200 MPa.
A compressive strength above approximately 200 MPa would be similar to or greater than strengths reported for epoxy-modified samples.
Copper infiltration will markedly suppress crack formation relative to the unchanged alloy.

The infiltrated composite's isothermal entropy change or adiabatic temperature change will remain within approximately 10% of the unchanged alloy under matched applied-field and pressure-field cycling.
Copper infiltration will increase thermal conductivity relative to the unchanged alloy.
Increasing copper content above 30 vol% could dilute the active caloric phase and compromise caloric performance.
The alloy's caloric transformation operates from near room temperature to moderately elevated temperatures.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says the intervention will not degrade caloric response, whereas the predicted outcome permits degradation of up to approximately 10%.
